newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament votes no changes to Red Square.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament votes no changes to Red Square.

text.p: Russia's lower house of parliament, worried by calls to move Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin's embalmed body out of Red Square, passed a draft law on Wednesday banning changes to the Moscow landmark.
"Reconstruction of sites situated on Red Square or any new construction there, which could change its historical face...are banned," said the draft approved by the State Duma by 253 votes to 48.

The draft now has to be considered by President Boris Yeltsin. It did not specifically mention Lenin's mausoleum, which lies under the Kremlin walls, or the embalmed body of the Bolshevik revolutionary who died in 1924.

But communist authors and liberal opponents of the draft made no secret that the fate of the mausoleum and Lenin's corpse was on their minds following renewed public debate over whether the late communist leader should be given a Christian burial.

Russian liberals, who blame the Bolshevik revolution of 1917 for putting the country on the wrong track for more than seven decades, see the reburial of Lenin's body and the destruction of the mausoleum as a symbol of the country she aking off its past.

The liberals say Lenin, whom they hold responsible for reprisals in the earky years of communist rule, still deserves a Christian burial next to his relatives at an Orthodox cemetery in St Petersburg rather than the fate of a tourist attraction.

The communists, for whom the founder of the now defunct Soviet Union is a sacred figure, say their political opponents' arguments are undermined by the fact that the embalmed bodies of Russian saints are still exhibited in some churches.

The communists also say that Lenin's tomb is part of the architectural ensemble of Red Square, listed among the world's historical heritage by the United Nations Educational, Science and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO).
Yeltsin, who spearheaded opposition to Soviet communist rule which collapsed in 1991, has been cautious in touching on the fate of Lenin's tomb and body.
But earlier this year he suggested that a referendum be held on the future of the mausoleum, triggering the latest bout of public debates.
